item.title: Police revise Rangpur family murder account as new questions emerge
item.description:
Police have revised key elements of their account of the murder of retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty and three members of his family, changing details about where and how the victims were killed while introducing land-related resentment as another possible motive.
The new account came Thursday amid growing public scepticism over the sensational killings, with teachers, former students and residents having already questioned the police version.
Rangpur Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mohammad Abdul Mabud said Ganapati, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, and daughter Agami Chakraborty, 25, were killed on the open third-floor terrace of their Machuapara home.
The bodies of the two women were then moved inside the rooftop entrance to conceal them from neighbours, he said.
Their 12-year-old son Ayush was killed after waking up and seeing one of the suspects inside the house.
That differs from the account police gave Sunday, when they said Ganapati was killed on the roof, his wife and daughter on the staircase and Ayush while he was asleep.
Explaining the discrepancy, Mabud said the suspects later told the court that Ayush had awakened and recognised Siddhartha Das.
According to police, Siddhartha and Mugdha Das had consumed eight yaba pills behind a rooftop water tank before Ganapati confronted them early in the morning. The pair then allegedly strangled him with a towel.
When Pritilata and Agami came upstairs after hearing the commotion, they too were strangled, police said.
The suspects allegedly later cut the house’s electricity connection, fearing the presence of CCTV cameras.
After entering the house, they encountered Ayush, who asked Siddhartha why he was there. Police said the boy was then suffocated to prevent him from raising an alarm.
Post-mortem examinations have confirmed that all four victims died from strangulation, according to the commissioner. He said tests found no evidence of rape.
Police have also broadened their investigation into the motive.
While initially attributing the killings to Ganapati’s objection to drug use on his rooftop, investigators are now examining possible resentment involving land purchased by Ganapati’s family from Siddhartha’s ancestors and alleged disputes over distribution of the proceeds.
Police are also examining whether social tensions between Ganapati’s Brahmin family and residents belonging largely to the Das community played any role.
Questions over the shifting account dominated Thursday’s press conference.
However, the commissioner left after answering only two questions, prompting protests from journalists seeking clarification over the changes in the police narrative.
The bodies of Ganapati, Pritilata, Agami and Ayush were recovered from their Rangpur home Saturday night.
Police maintain that Siddhartha and Mugdha carried out all four killings, while the investigation into the motive continues.

item.title: Opposition MPs walk out of parliament over reform process
item.description:
Opposition lawmakers walked out of parliament on Thursday, the opening day of the third session of the 13th Parliament, protesting what they described as a unilateral approach to bills and constitutional reforms.
At around 8:07pm, lawmakers from the 11-party opposition alliance, including Jamaat-e-Islami and the National Citizen Party (NCP), left the chamber following a speech by Opposition Leader Dr Shafiqur Rahman.
Speaking as the House began proceedings to introduce three government bills, Shafiqur raised concerns over public suffering caused by the electricity and gas crises and rising prices of essential commodities.
He also questioned the process surrounding the bills, constitutional amendments and reforms before announcing that opposition lawmakers would not participate in the proceedings.
“We knew that private members’ day was meant for private members. But we are seeing that Parliament is being pushed towards a one-sided and unilateral course on everything,” he said.
“We do not want to participate in such bills as a matter of principle. We believe such actions will suppress the main demand for reforms. We are not in favour of suppressing that demand,” he added.
Reiterating his party’s position on reforms, Shafiqur said: “We are firmly and clearly in favour of the main demand for reforms. We have not moved from that position—officially or unofficially.”
The opposition leader also questioned the process of forming the constitutional amendment committee.
“We have repeatedly been requested, both inside and outside Parliament, to join the constitutional amendment committee. A committee was passed here. We protested and did not participate,” he said.
Shafiqur said the opposition later questioned whether there was any provision for forming a committee under that name.
“Later, when we said there was no provision for forming a committee called the Constitutional Amendment Committee, we heard that a particular word had been added before it. I do not know whether that particular wording was passed here,” he said.
Questioning the procedure, he said: “If a committee is actually passed by this House, then every letter of it must also be passed from here. That was not done. We were not in favour of it. That is not the main issue. I am saying that the procedure was not followed here.”

item.title: Khalilur: No reason for others to be concerned over Makkah Pact
item.description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman on Thursday said there is no reason for other countries or communities to be concerned if the Saudi Arabia-Türkiye-Pakistan “Makkah Pact” is expanded, describing it as a mechanism for the self-defense of the global Muslim community and an internal matter among Muslim countries.
“There is no reason for others to have any concern over it,” he said while replying to a supplementary question from independent lawmaker Rumeen Farhana in parliament on Thursday regarding the possible benefits for Bangladesh if it joins the pact.
The foreign minister said Bangladesh’s possible participation in the arrangement is not an issue at this stage, as the matter would depend primarily on the intentions of the countries currently involved in the pact.
“If they express an intention to invite Bangladesh to join this pact, we will certainly have to consider the matter,” he said.
He added that it would be premature to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of Bangladesh joining the arrangement before any such invitation is made.
“We will certainly keep all these matters under consideration,” the minister said. The foreign minister said the pact was signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan on August 7, 2026 while the three countries’ initiative was being viewed positively by Bangladesh.
However, he stressed that any decision regarding Bangladesh’s participation would depend on whether the existing members wished to invite Bangladesh to join.
The foreign minister also said that, if expanded, the pact should be understood in the context of collective self-defense among Muslim countries.
He described it as an internal matter of the Muslim community and said there should be no cause for concern among others over such an arrangement.
Replying to another supplementary question from Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami lawmaker Mir Ahmad Binquasem, the foreign minister also said Bangladesh would use its presidency of the United Nations General Assembly to serve all 193 member states rather than pursue the interests of any particular country.
He said the UNGA presidency was a position representing all members of the world body.
“After winning the election, I said I would work as the President of all countries,” he said.
Citing an example with the Speaker’s role in parliament, he said, “Just as you are the Speaker of all members of parliament, I will serve as the president of the general assembly, which represents all UN member states.”
He stressed that there was very little scope for the UNGA President to work for the interests of a particular country.
“I request all of you to take this into consideration. Bangladesh will proudly discharge this responsibility for everyone,” he said.
Recalling Bangladesh’s campaign for the UNGA presidency, the foreign minister said the achievement was particularly significant because of the short time available for preparation.
He said when the prime minister nominated him for the position, only five countries had entered the contest.
He said Bangladesh’s Asian competitor had around 10 years to prepare for the contest, while he had only about 10 weeks.
“I told the prime minister that you have sent me on an impossible mission,” he recalled.
The prime minister, however, told him: “You will get it; together we will achieve it.”
The foreign minister credited the prime minister’s leadership and collective efforts for Bangladesh’s success and expressed his special gratitude to the prime minister.
He said the presidency of the UN General Assembly ultimately belonged to all 193 member states and Bangladesh would discharge the responsibility in a manner that reflected the interests of the wider international community.

item.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: Death toll climbs to 362; over 1,400 missing
item.description:
Rescue teams waded through mud on Thursday searching for more than 1,400 people missing after flash floods and landslides struck the Nepal-Tibet border, as the death toll rose sharply to at least 362, with entire villages swept away.
Experts warned of the risk of further floods a day after the devastating tsunami-like wall of freezing water and mud wiped out towns under a torrent of sludge, engulfing homes, smashing bridges and dams, and sweeping vehicles away like toys.
Many of the missing are foreign tourists, including scores of Hindu pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred snow-capped Mount Kailash.
According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered a vast flow of icy debris.
Emergency teams were racing to pluck survivors from affected zones, while Nepali soldiers used sniffer dogs to search for bodies buried under the suffocating dirt.
“Everything is finished,” Omkar Joshi, a 35-year-old Nepali customs agent rescued from a hilltop in the border town of Timure, told AFP.
“It is a giant graveyard. All that is left are sand and pebbles, soaked red by human blood.”
Nepali police said they had recovered 359 bodies.
Another 910 people, including 517 foreign tourists, were out of contact in the country. Beijing said 100 Chinese citizens are missing in Nepal.
In China, state media said the “mudslide disaster” at the Gyirong Port in Tibet killed three people, while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, are missing.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited the area on Thursday, state media said, to oversee “emergency rescue and relief work, and to visit rescue workers and affected people.”
Li Qipu, a member of China’s paramilitary People’s Armed Police, cited “the instability of a reservoir lake upstream” and “the narrow mountain road” as elements complicating rescue efforts.
China’s Tibet Autonomous Region is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who urged the Himalayan nation to “stand together” hours after the disaster, visited some of the hardest-hit areas on Thursday.
Shah told local authorities to “provide immediate relief to displaced families” and to open blocked roads, his office said in a statement.
The foreigners out of contact included Indians and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea and the United States, Nepal’s tourism board said.
The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami”, travelling nearly 170 kilometers (105 miles) south into Nepal, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble, of Australia’s La Trobe University.
Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected, but deaths were reported as far south as Chitwan, on the border with India.
Buddhist spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, who lives in exile in India, said he would “pray for all those who have lost their lives.”
Chinese government officials in Tibet mobilized nearly 800 emergency workers, as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, the official Xinhua news agency said.
Promises of aid and assistance came in soon after reports of the scale of the disaster.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was sending emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags.
The USGS said the flood was sparked by a glacial collapse, which caused seismic activity and the “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
“This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake,” it said, but the seismic recordings were analyzed and it was found instead to be a “glacial collapse and debris flow.”
Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses.
Fears of more potential floods remain, with water trapped by the immense piles of debris blocking the valley.
“With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur,” said Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.
Katmandu’s Flood Forecasting Division issued a “special notice” on Thursday, warning of a growing lake behind debris left by the landslide.
“Residents of downstream areas of the Bhote Koshi River, travelers, rescue personnel, and all concerned are requested to exercise extreme caution,” it said.
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among the hundreds missing on the border, Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru said on Thursday.
They were returning from a holy pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, on the Chinese side of the frontier, when they were caught in the floods at an immigration post.
“The entire group was there in the building,” Sadhguru said in a video message to his millions of followers, weeping as he spoke from Tibet, with the anguished wails of other pilgrims heard in the background.
“This is a terrible and extraordinary event.”

item.title: Foreign minister: Bangladesh buries submissive diplomacy, won't bow to anyone
item.description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman on Thursday said Bangladesh has buried the submissive foreign policy of the past and will never bow to any country again.
Responding to a supplementary question from Naogaon-3 lawmaker Md Fazley Houda during the question-answer session in parliament, the minister outlined the government’s foreign policy.
“Thanks to the strong and successful foreign policy pursued by our honorable prime minister, we are now standing tall with our heads held high,” he said.
“Under the prime minister’s leadership, we will continue to pursue this foreign policy, and Bangladesh will never again bow its head before anyone. We have buried the submissive foreign policy,” Khalilur said.
Referring to the previous Awami League regime, he said Bangladesh’s foreign policy had, to a large extent, not remained under its own control during the 15 years of what he described as misrule.
The minister said the government is now preparing key performance indicators for every Bangladeshi mission abroad and will evaluate their performance accordingly.
“We will place all the relevant information before parliament when we present the next budget. You have the right to know this information,” he said.
Replying to another supplementary question from Bagerhat-4 lawmaker Md Abdul Aleem, Khalilur said Bangladesh remains active in pursuing its fair share of water from common rivers.
He said a team has been formed to prepare a new agreement following the expiry of the Ganges Water-sharing Treaty, and the Indian authorities have been informed accordingly. “We are now waiting for their response,” he said.
The minister said Bangladesh has started a technical evaluation with China regarding the Teesta project, adding that further steps will be taken based on the outcome of the assessment.
The third session of the current parliament began at 3:00pm with Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad in the chair.
The first hour of the day’s proceedings was devoted to the question-answer session.

item.title: Bodies of nine Bangladeshis killed in Riyadh factory fire arrive
item.description:
The bodies of nine of the 16 Bangladeshis killed in a devastating fire at a sofa factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, were brought back to Bangladesh on Thursday.
The bodies arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka aboard Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight BG-430 in the afternoon.
Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury and State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam were present at the airport to receive the bodies.
The fire broke out at the sofa factory in Riyadh on August 9, killing 16 Bangladeshi workers. The identities of nine victims were confirmed through fingerprint tests before their bodies were repatriated.
Seven of the victims were from Atrai upazila in Naogaon. They were identified as Md Farid of Udanpoy village; Rubel Pramanik, Kalimuddin Islam, Mohon Ali and his younger brother Sumon Ali of Gondogohali village; Sohel Rana of Dubai village; and Abdul Jalil Sarker of Parkasunda village.
The other two victims were Rabiul Islam of Mahishdanga village in Naldanga, Natore, and Shyamal Uddin of Morugram village in Bagmara, Rajshahi.
According to reports, the workers were sleeping inside the factory after finishing their work when the fire broke out. The factory’s main gate was allegedly locked from outside, preventing them from escaping. All 16 workers were trapped and died in the blaze.
At a press briefing at the airport, Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said fingerprint tests could not be conducted on the remaining seven victims. DNA samples have been collected from their relatives under CID supervision, and efforts are underway to repatriate their bodies as soon as possible.
The government has decided to provide Tk 335,000 to each family of the nine deceased workers. The amount includes Tk 35,000 for transportation and burial expenses and Tk 300,000 as a one-time financial grant.
The Wage Earners’ Welfare Board has also arranged ambulances to transport the bodies directly to their respective village homes. State Minister Shama Obaed Islam said embassy officials in Saudi Arabia were working tirelessly to bring home the remaining victims.
“Bangladeshi migrant workers leave home, endure difficult working conditions and send money to support their families,” she said, adding that efforts were underway to complete the DNA identification process and repatriate the remaining bodies at the earliest.

item.title: Nazrul’s 50th death anniversary observed
item.description:
The 50th death anniversary of national poet Kazi Nazrul Islam was observed on Thursday.
Nazrul, revered as Bidrohi Kobi (a rebel poet) for his activism for political and social justice, breathed his last in Dhaka on 12th Bhadro of the Bangla calendar year 1383 (August 29, 1976) at the age of 77. He was buried with full state honours beside the Dhaka University (DU) Central Mosque.
Nazrul produced a large volume of poetry and music with themes that included religious devotion and spiritual rebellion against all sorts of oppression.
Different socio-cultural and political organizations arranged elaborate programs on the occasion. Television channels aired special programs on his works and life to observe the day.
The programs started with Qurankhwani after Fajr prayers at the DU Central Mosque by different organizations, while a discussion was held on the campus.
Later, DU teachers and students and other political and socio-cultural organizations placed wreaths at the grave of the national poet in the morning.
Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy organized a two-day program marking the death anniversary of the national poet.
Kazi Nazrul Islam was born on May 24, 1899, in Churulia village in Asansol subdivision of Burdwan district of West Bengal, India.
Following Bangladesh’s independence, Nazrul was brought to Dhaka with his family on May 24, 1972, with special permission from the government of India.
He was given the status of National Poet, provided with state accommodation in Dhanmondi, awarded an honorary D Litt by Dhaka University in 1974, and granted Bangladeshi citizenship in 1976. The same year, he was honoured with the Ekushey Padak.
Meanwhile, BNP acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi Ahmed on Thursday said National Poet Kazi Nazrul Islam was an inspiration behind all major movements in Bangladesh from the country’s independence war to the 2024 mass uprising.
He made the remarks after paying tribute to Kazi Nazrul Islam at the poet’s grave on the Dhaka University campus in the morning.

item.title: Uproar over home minister’s remarks disrupts Parliament proceedings
item.description:
The third session of the 13th Parliament turned heated on its opening day on Thursday as opposition lawmakers protested remarks made by Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed during the question-answer session, triggering loud protests and disrupting proceedings for around 10 minutes.
Opposition lawmakers strongly objected to what they described as disparaging remarks by the minister. Although Salahuddin later withdrew the remarks, the situation did not immediately calm.
Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad repeatedly urged the opposition lawmakers to take their seats and allow the minister to speak.
Later, expressing concern over what he described as growing intolerance among lawmakers, the speaker said he was “somewhat concerned” about the future of Parliament.
The incident began when Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami lawmaker Md Shafiqul Islam Masud, while asking a supplementary question, alleged that snatching incidents are taking place in broad daylight and that lawmakers are being attacked.
He also alleged that opposition leaders and activists are being arrested in false cases, while accused persons in cases involving attacks on opposition members are not being arrested.
Masud asked what steps the home minister is taking in this regard.
Initially, Salahuddin said he was inattentive during the first minute and asked Masud to repeat his question.
After Masud repeated it, the minister said, “Speaking at Shahbagh Square and speaking in Parliament are not the same thing.”
The remark immediately drew strong protests from opposition lawmakers, many of whom stood up and began shouting.
Earlier, while replying to a question from National Citizen Party (NCP) lawmaker Hasnat Abdullah, Salahuddin said: “I could not understand whether this is a question or a speech at Paltan.”
Although some lawmakers mildly objected to that remark, the reaction became much stronger after his response to Masud’s question.
Facing the protests, the minister said he did not direct the remark at anyone.
As the commotion continued, he told the speaker: “I am seeking your shelter.”
Amid the uproar, the home minister eventually said he was withdrawing his remarks. But the opposition members continued their protest, forcing him to sit down at one point as he could not be heard over the noise.
The speaker repeatedly urged the lawmakers to remain seated and listen to the minister.
"Honourable members, that is enough. You have spoken for a long time. Now please sit down. Please take your seats," he was heard saying.
Hafiz Uddin also told the opposition members that they will be given an opportunity to speak through their microphones instead of shouting from their seats.
"This is not the Awami League's time. Here you can criticise the government as much as you want. Please sit down and wait," he said.
The Speaker assured the opposition that he will give the opposition leader the floor after the home minister completed his statement.
Salahuddin then resumed speaking, while the opposition lawmakers continued standing and protesting. The Speaker urged him to address the Chair.
Amid the continued uproar, Salahuddin said questions about where snatching took place and whether accused persons were arrested should be raised specifically rather than making wholesale remarks.
Speaker Hafiz Uddin subsequently gave the floor to Opposition Leader Dr Shafiqur Rahman.
As some treasury bench lawmakers began making comments, Shafiqur responded: "Will you give the speech, or will I? You give it."
Addressing the speaker, he said: "This is ominous. If comments are made like this while I am speaking, then there is no need for me to stand here."
The Speaker then asked him to continue.
Shafiqur said: "With due respect to the honourable members of Parliament and the home minister, I want to say he has not used these words for the first time today. Since the Parliament began its session, he has been belittling everyone. I do not understand what he thinks of himself."
He further alleged that Salahuddin had previously shown the "audacity" to say in Parliament that he would play the role of a teacher.
"We did not come here to become his students. If he wants to teach, let him open a university. Those who like it can enrol there and listen to his lectures," the opposition leader said.
He said the home minister "attacked" the opposition twice in the same sitting.
"My colleagues think, and I also think, that this is not cultural; this is parliamentary fascism. This should not happen," he said.
Demanding that the home minister apologize and that his remarks be expunged from the parliamentary record, Shafiqur said the opposition will remain in the House if those demands are met. "Otherwise, there is no question of sitting here with this humiliation," he said.
Opposition lawmakers thumped their desks in support of their leader.
Later, Speaker Hafiz Uddin said all lawmakers are working to reflect the hopes and aspirations of the people in Parliament.
He said Parliament cannot function effectively if its Rules of Procedure are not followed.
"I am deeply saddened to observe that I am increasingly noticing intolerance among some members," the Speaker said.
He reminded lawmakers that Parliament has been elected for five years and that everyone has the right to speak.
Hafiz Uddin said the home minister's remarks will be examined and any unparliamentary words will be expunged, if necessary.
"But do not take away the freedom of speech. There are twice or three times as many members on this side (the treasury bench) as there are on your (opposition) side. So, the message cannot be silenced by making noise. Let me run the Parliament," he told the opposition.
In response, Opposition Leader Shafiqur said the issue was already clear and did not require further examination.
He also objected to the Speaker's reference to the numerical strength of the two sides. "I did not like it when, towards the end, you said that there are three times as many members on this side than on that side. I am not in favour of dividing this Parliament by any ratio," he said.
"We have said from the beginning that we will all unite for good work and work together. If anything wrong happens, we will protest," Shafiqur said.
Later, ruling party lawmaker Md Manirul Haque Chowdhury spoke on a point of order.
After his remarks, Speaker Hafiz Uddin expressed concern over the way lawmakers prevented one another from speaking.
"Honourable Members of Parliament, I am somewhat concerned about the future of Parliament. Today, I have observed attempts to prevent one another from speaking. This is not a good sign for Parliament," he said.
The speaker said democracy has been achieved after much struggle. “Every member of Parliament has a responsibility to ensure that this democracy remains intact.”

item.title: Yayoi Kusama, ‘queen of polka dot’ dies at 97
item.description:
Yayoi Kusama, one of the world’s most celebrated contemporary artists, died at 97, her company announced Thursday, prompting tributes from around the world.
Known as the “polka dot queen”, the Japanese artist transformed decades of hallucinations and mental health struggles into vibrant works defined by her signature dots, nets and infinity motifs. Her career spanned continents and disciplines, from painting and performance to fiction and poetry.
Kusama’s company said she died in a hospital in Tokyo, announcing her death on August 14. “She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush,” the company said in a statement, adding that she remained focused throughout her life on themes of “forever love and eternal soul”.
Born in 1929 to a wealthy and conservative family, Kusama began producing her distinctive art at age 10. In her autobiography, she recalled seeing a red flower pattern from a tablecloth spread across the ceiling, windows and pillars of a room — an experience that shaped her lifelong artistic vocabulary.
After studying art in Japan, Kusama moved to the United States in the late 1950s. With encouragement from artist Georgia O’Keeffe, she became a fixture of New York’s avant-garde scene, gaining recognition for large-scale paintings and provocative happenings in the 1960s.
Her performances combined body painting with polka dots, while she faced discrimination as both a Japanese immigrant and a woman in a male-dominated art world.
Kusama also launched a fashion line, founded a group she called the “Church of Self-Obliteration” and, styling herself the “High Priestess of Polka Dots”, officiated at a gay wedding.
Kusama returned to Japan in the 1970s and voluntarily entered a Tokyo psychiatric hospital, where she lived and continued to work for the rest of her life.
Her profile rose again from the 1980s onward, and she became instantly recognisable in her bright red wig and boldly spotted outfits.
Her infinity mirror rooms and pumpkin sculptures, including a well-known installation on the Japanese art island of Naoshima, continued to draw large crowds. Her immersive exhibitions also helped cement her global reputation, while her works sold for millions of dollars at auction.
At the Yayoi Kusama Museum in Tokyo, visitors gathered Thursday after news of her death broke.
Ai Kono, 50, told AFP she had travelled from Yokohama with her 10-year-old daughter to see Kusama’s work when she learned of the artist’s passing. She described Kusama as a woman of persistence who lived a long and fulfilling life.
Apple CEO Tim Cook also paid tribute on social media platform X, describing Kusama as a visionary whose work expanded the boundaries of contemporary art and left the world more vibrant.

item.title: 10,000 cases filed to recover loans of Sammilito Islami Bank
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has reviewed the progress of loan recovery, restructuring, and overall operations of Sammilito Islami Bank PLC.
Prioritizing defaulted loan recovery to safeguard depositors' interests, the bank has already filed around 10,000 lawsuits, with the process underway to file more.
On Thursday (August 27), the overall progress of the bank was reviewed during a meeting between Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostakur Rahman and the central bank's bank resolution department.
The meeting discussed the merger and restructuring of the bank, reorganization of the board of directors and management, human resource adjustments, branch integration, as well as the alignment of IT and operational activities.
These initiatives are being implemented under the guidance and supervision of Bangladesh Bank, while the BRD is regularly monitoring and following up on the progress.
It was informed during the meeting that alongside conventional legal actions to recover defaulted loans, the bank has also initiated compromise-based measures through an alternative loan settlement policy and Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms.
Meanwhile, a forensic audit is in its final stages to identify individuals involved in irregularities, corruption, loan fraud, and asset misappropriation that occurred under the bank's previous ownership and management.
Over the past six months, several major steps have been taken to restructure and coordinate the bank's activities.
The Board of Directors has been reconstituted with a focus on independent directors. A new CEO was appointed on July 16.
Work has been finalized to realign the designations, responsibilities, and organizational structure of nearly 16,000 officers and employees to manage the merged operations of five banks.
Progress is ongoing to integrate Core Banking Systems (CBS), Swift for international transactions, and related IT infrastructure to bring the operations of all five banks under a unified framework.
A unified system has been established, allowing depositors to withdraw funds from any branch across the five banks.
Operational integration, reorganization, and consolidation are currently underway for 780 branches and 1,500 business units based on location, business potential, customer service, and operating costs.
Bangladesh Bank stated that it is closely monitoring the progress of Sammilito Islami Bank's restructuring, loan recovery, case resolution, HR management, branch/business unit mergers, and technological integration.
The central bank expects that these combined measures will enhance the bank's governance, operational efficiency, and financial capacity.
Furthermore, it will accelerate loan recovery, reduce operational costs, and help re-channel stuck funds back into productive sectors.
Starting its journey as Bangladesh's largest state-owned Shariah-based bank with a capital of Tk35,000 crore, ensuring transparency, accountability, and good governance in managing Sammilito Islami Bank PLC's assets and deposits remains a top priority for Bangladesh Bank.

item.title: Three snakes found on 19th floor of secretariat
item.description:
Three snakes were found in the corridor of the Education Ministry on the 19th floor of Building No 6 at Bangladesh Secretariat on Thursday, raising questions about how they reached such a high floor.
Officials and employees first spotted two snakes in the corridor after arriving at work in the morning. Another snake was seen in the same area a short while later.
The offices of the education minister and education secretary are located on the same floor.
Officials who witnessed the incident said the snakes were seen moving through the corridor, causing panic among ministry officials and employees.
Ministry employees later killed all three snakes.
However, their species could not be immediately identified.
The ministry’s public relations officials confirmed the incident on Thursday afternoon and expressed surprise at finding three snakes together on the 19th floor of the Secretariat.
They said there could be more snakes inside a storeroom or elsewhere in the building, adding to concerns among officials and employees.
The incident has also raised questions about how the snakes managed to reach the 19th floor and whether there are other snakes inside the building.

item.title: Speaker: Disorder could threaten parliament’s functioning
item.description:
Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad Bir Bikram has warned that continued shouting, discourteous behavior and violations of parliamentary rules could seriously threaten Parliament’s functioning.
He made the remarks during the third session of the 13th National Parliament on Thursday following a commotion and exchange of words over statements by Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed and the opposition leader.
“The Rules of Procedure must be strictly followed to keep the democracy achieved through many sacrifices functioning and to make this institution of the people effective,” he said.
“The opposition has full freedom to point out the shortcomings and lapses of the government. But shouting in unison and silencing a minister without allowing him to finish his statement cannot be a healthy parliamentary practice.”
Recalling his nearly 40 years of parliamentary experience, the speaker referred to the bitter history of the past and urged lawmakers to learn from it and work toward building a better Parliament.
The opposition leader later resumed the discussion, referring to past instances in which statements were removed from parliamentary proceedings or sent for review.
He said the home minister’s remarks were clearly unparliamentary and alleged that similar incidents had occurred repeatedly.
He also questioned the speaker’s impartiality and protested the Speaker’s remarks that the treasury bench had more members.
The opposition leader said he did not support dividing Parliament based on numbers or status. He said the opposition would support the government on good initiatives and protest against wrongdoing.
He expressed hope that the speaker would conduct proceedings impartially and ensure equal dignity for all lawmakers.
Lawmaker Md Manirul Haque Chowdhury raised a point of order after part of his budget speech was removed from the proceedings for telling a metaphorical story.
He asked the speaker which word in his statement had been deemed unparliamentary.
Manirul also alleged that remarks about his beard and religious beliefs had undermined his personal dignity and the dignity of Parliament.
Seeking protection of his dignity, he asked the Speaker to respond formally to the notice and sought a resolution and ruling on the matter.
Responding to the overall situation, Hafiz Uddin said he had not been present when the incident involving Manirul occurred and would review the proceedings.
He said necessary action would be taken if anything unparliamentary was found.
“It is extremely regrettable that members are being prevented from speaking in the way they are,” he said.
The Speaker warned that Parliament could not function for long if lawmakers failed to follow his direction to sit down when asked.
Expressing disappointment over the disorder, he urged all sides to exercise patience.
The session was later adjourned for Asr prayers.

item.description:

Against this backdrop, the ministers, state ministers and whips have been given the responsibility of supervising and coordinating district-level activities related to law and order, corruption and drug control, good governance, transparency and accountability, as well as development and public welfare programs.

item.title: Kader Gani Chowdhury appointed BSS MD, chief editor
item.description:
The government has appointed senior journalist Muhammad Kader Gani Chowdhury as managing director and chief editor of the state-run news agency Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS).
The Ministry of Public Administration issued a gazette notification in this regard on Thursday.
According to the notification, Kader Gani Chowdhury has been appointed under the Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha Act, 2018, on a contractual basis for one year.
His appointment will take effect from the date of his joining and is subject to his relinquishing any employment or professional engagement with any other profession, business, or government, semi-government, or private institution or organization.
Kader Gani Chowdhury replaces Md Kamal Uddin Mozumder, better known as Kamal Uddin Shabuj, who was appointed BSS managing director and chief editor on April 7.
Kader Gani Chowdhury has long been involved in journalism. He is currently serving as secretary general of the Bangladesh Federal Union of Journalists (BFUJ), the apex platform of journalists in Bangladesh.

item.title: ACC sues ex-land minister, 28 others over Tk141C Aramit Cement scam
item.description:
The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) has filed three cases against former land minister Saifuzzaman Chowdhury and 28 others over the alleged embezzlement and laundering of Tk 141 crore through Aramit Cement.
The cases accuse the defendants of withdrawing funds from Islami Bank’s Jubilee Road branch in Chittagong using fake bills and vouchers for the purported purchase of cement raw materials, despite no actual transactions. The funds were allegedly transferred and converted through various bank accounts before being laundered to the UAE, UK, US and other countries.
ACC Deputy Director and Public Relations Officer Aktarul Islam disclosed the information on Thursday.
The accused include Saifuzzaman Chowdhury, his wife and Aramit Cement Managing Director Rukhmila Zaman, former UCB PLC chairperson; Aramit Cement CFO Mohammad Shah Alam; Imperial Trading proprietor Md Abdul Aziz; and officials of various banks and related institutions.
Of the 29 accused, 27 were named in the first case, 16 in the second and 20 in the third.
According to the case documents, Saifuzzaman allegedly used his influence as Aramit Group owner and then land minister to secure loan approvals, falsely portray an Aramit employee as the owner of a supplier, and facilitate the transfer, conversion and cash withdrawal of the funds before laundering them abroad.
He was also accused of purchasing assets in the UAE, UK, US and other countries with the laundered money and identified as the ultimate beneficiary and mastermind of the alleged scheme.
Rukhmila Zaman was accused of facilitating the transactions as UCB chairperson and Aramit Group managing director, using her influence to secure loan approvals and assisting in the transfer and laundering of the funds.
Aramit Cement CFO Mohammad Shah Alam and Imperial Trading proprietor Md Abdul Aziz were also accused of facilitating fake applications and deal approvals, as well as the transfer, conversion and cash withdrawal of the funds.
According to the ACC, the first incident took place on March 20, 2018. A case filed by ACC Assistant Director Sajib Ahmed accuses 16 people of embezzling Tk 57.60 crore through a deal in the name of Imperial Trading, a customer of First Security Islami Bank’s Agrabad branch, based on an application submitted by Aramit Cement’s Jubilee Road branch.
The second incident occurred between April 4, 2018 and December 26, 2019. According to the case documents, Tk 41.625 crore was allegedly embezzled through 17 deals in the name of Imperial Trading, a customer of United Commercial Bank’s Kamal Bazar branch, following an application by Aramit Cement, a customer of Islami Bank’s Jubilee Road branch. ACC Deputy Director Md Mashiur Rahman filed the case against 27 people.
The third incident took place between August 6, 2020 and March 28, 2021. According to the ACC, nine deals were made in the name of Imperial Trading, a customer of United Commercial Bank’s Sadarghat branch, based on applications from Aramit Cement. The case alleges that Tk 42.075 crore was embezzled after excluding the customer’s equity of Tk 4.675 crore. ACC official Shoaib Ibn Alam filed the case against 20 people.

item.title: Aid efforts trickle in after deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
item.description:
International aid organizations are scrambling to help victims of devastating floods and landslides on the Nepal-Tibet border.
The disaster has killed more than 360 people, with rescuers searching for 1,400 people reported missing.
UN relief chief Tom Fletcher said Thursday he had allocated $2 million “to save lives with emergency medical care, shelter, water” after the “horrifying flash floods.”
The World Health Organization (WHO) has sent medical kits to provide basic health services to 10,000 people for three months, while the World Food Program and UN children’s fund are readying relief supplies.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it had allocated more than $1 million.
“Many families have lost their homes,” IFRC chief in Nepal David Fisher told AFP, adding that whole settlements had been “wiped out.”
Mona Sherpa, head of Care Nepal, said her charity was worried about “the spread of waterborne diseases due to damaged water and sanitation infrastructure.”
Neighboring India sent a military cargo plane with aid hours after the disaster, with further planes flying in nearly 50 tons of supplies.
Delhi was also sending in steel Bailey bridges, with infrastructure washed out in Nepal.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi said earlier that India was “ready to provide all possible humanitarian assistance to Nepal.”
Bangladesh said it was sending tents, mosquito nets, food and body bags, according to a government statement.
Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said the island nation stood “ready to assist Nepal in rescue and clearance operations.”
The European Union said it had activated its Copernicus satellite surveillance system to help recovery efforts.
Japan was sending an emergency response team, while Switzerland has said it had allocated more than $600,000.
The US State Department said it was sending a disaster response advisor along with $500,000 in aid.

item.title: Iran, Qatar hold Hormuz talks as US blockade chokes Iran oil imports
item.description:
Iran’s top diplomat met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, as a US naval blockade squeezes oil supplies to Iran amid a domestic shortfall.
The visit by Qatar’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani follows a week of intense diplomacy in Iran involving separate meetings with Oman’s top diplomat and senior Pakistani officials seeking ways to end the Middle East war and reopen Hormuz.
It also comes as Washington threatens wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran, part of a broader campaign it has called “economic asphyxiation.”
Iranian state television said Al Thani, who is also Qatar’s prime minister, had met with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, without providing details.
Qatar’s foreign ministry said they discussed de-escalation efforts as well as the proposed framework for Hormuz between Iran and Oman.
Al Thani “emphasized the necessity of respecting the sovereignty of neighboring states and freedom of navigation,” and pursuing dialogue, the ministry said.
Alongside mediator Pakistan, Qatar had played a key role in securing an April ceasefire and June deal between Iran and the United States, but those deals have since collapsed.
Since war with the United States broke out on February 28, Iran has maintained tight control over Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, with Washington imposing a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Vice President Mohammad Jafar Ghaempanah said the blockade had prevented his country from importing enough petrol to cover a shortfall in domestic production.
“Petrol production is insufficient, and because of the US naval blockade, we cannot import it,” he was quoted by the official IRNA news agency as saying.
In recent days, many Iranians have been seen queuing outside petrol stations. Presidential chief of staff Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei meanwhile said petrol quotas would be reviewed, without elaborating.
Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world’s cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidized petrol, making changes to pricing politically sensitive.
As the United States seeks to strangle Iran’s economy, Iranian officials have dismissed the measures as “failed policies” that will not force Tehran to change course.
“The country is in an all-out economic war,” said Iran’s top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf in a statement carried by local media.
“We will see that the government... will defeat the enemy on this ground as well,” he added.
Even before the war, Iran’s economy was battered by decades of international sanctions, and has long suffered from chronic inflation and a weakening currency.
Iran has for weeks been in talks with Oman, which also overlooks the Hormuz strait, over a framework agreement that would establish a “temporary corridor” for shipping and provide for clearing mines Tehran says were laid during the war.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Wednesday said the two countries had agreed on each country’s share of the waters and any revenues collected from managing the waterway.
Tehran has nonetheless insisted that the strait will not be reopened unless Washington meets its demands, including lifting its naval blockade, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad and removing oil sanctions.
Since the war broke out, Iranian forces have required vessels to obtain permission to transit the waterway and struck ships that failed to comply.
Tehran has also sought to impose service fees on ships using the strait -- a move strongly opposed by Washington and regional countries.
On Thursday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said an “unknown projectile” had struck a tanker in Hormuz this week, causing a fire that was later extinguished.

item.title: Could Syria become the focus of an Israeli-Turkish conflict?
item.description:
Following US mediation, Syrian and Israeli representatives met in Jordan last weekend for the first time in months. The talks aimed to defuse tensions following the recent Israeli attacks on Syrian territory and prevent hostilities between Israel and Turkiye from spilling over into Syria.
The escalation was sparked by an Israeli attack on the Abu Duhur military airfield in Syria’s Idlib Province on August 18. According to Syrian sources, the attack struck the runway and storage facilities without causing any fatalities. Israel stated that Syria had violated — or threatened to violate — a previous security agreement by allowing Turkish troops to use the airfield. The governments of both Syria and Turkiye rejected these allegations.
The United States criticized the attack by its Israeli ally as an “unnecessary escalation.” In diplomatic terms, this amounts to a fairly clear show of rhetorical support for Ankara and Damascus.
Israel views a potential Turkish military presence in Syria as a red line. Yet, it remains unclear whether such a deployment is planned in the long term or whether it was even imminent at the time of the attack. Evidence on this matter is not publicly available.
However, as early as April 2025, Reuters news agency cited anonymous sources saying Turkiye had inspected at least three air bases in Syria where it might want to station troops as part of a planned joint defense pact. Israeli airstrikes were already taking place at that time as well.
The Washington-based think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), which is considered pro-Israel, justifies the attack as follows: “Israel worries that Ankara could eventually use its military presence in Syria as a platform to pressure or threaten Israel, and remains wary of the close relationship between Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa and the Turkish leadership.”
For Bente Scheller, Syria expert at the German Green Party-affiliated Heinrich Böll Foundation, this explanation falls short.
“There is no evidence so far that Turkish troops are actually supposed to be stationed there,” she told DW. While Israel may indeed have its own intelligence, the recent attack must be viewed against the backdrop of Israel’s overall policy toward Syria as well as Turkiye’s growing regional role, she noted.
Marcus Schneider, a Middle East analyst at Germany’s Friedrich Ebert Foundation — which is affiliated with the German Social Democratic Party (SPD) — in Beirut, also points out that a struggle for power and influence is unfolding in Syria and beyond.
“The attack primarily raises the question of what kind of military order will emerge in Syria in the future,” he told DW. In his view, Israel wants to keep Syria weak, as a sovereign state that controls its own airspace would restrict Israel’s military freedom of action. “The corridor for attacks against Iran runs through Syria,” explained Schneider. A sovereign Syria could therefore pose a strategic obstacle to Israel.
Following the Hamas terror attacks on Israel on October 7, Israel’s heightened security concerns are understandable, adds Scheller. In addition, Israel is certainly viewing with concern another development that extends beyond Syria.
“Israel is undoubtedly aware of how Turkiye is currently attempting to position itself as a regional hegemon,” Scheller said. The attack on Abu al-Duhur is therefore “clearly also a message to Turkiye.”
Turkiye supports Syrian President al-Sharaa and is committed to a unified Syria which includes the territory in the country’s northeast, where the majority of Syria’s Kurdish population is located. For years, Turkiye has been attacking the former Kurdish-led autonomous zone along its southern border. On Tuesday, the commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces announced the official dissolution of the group.
An analysis by the US think tank Carnegie Foundation describes the situation as a strategic rivalry between Israel and Turkiye: “The northeast is also the main arena where two externally driven strategic visions for Syria collide.” The International Crisis Group also views Syria as a fault line between Turkiye, a rising regional power, and Israel.
Syria’s improved relations with the US — which amount to US support — offer new prospects for the country, despite the Islamist past of its new leader, President Ahmad al-Sharaa. In summer 2025, the US began gradually easing sanctions, and in November of that year, al-Sharaa was received by US President Trump at the White House. The two met again on the sidelines of the Nato summit in Ankara in July 2026. In early 2026, the US withdrew its military forces from Syria, and on Monday (August 24), it officially removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
However, under the current circumstances, Syria appears to be relying primarily on itself, including in its relations with Turkiye. For analyst Marcus Schneider, however, a potential Turkish presence is not comparable to the former Iranian presence during the Assad regime.
Contrary to the view held in Israel, he argues that Ankara is primarily interested in a stable Syria and in securing its southern border. “The idea that Turkiye, a Nato member, would attack Israel, a nuclear power, is preposterous,” he said. The real problem, he argues, is that Israel increasingly views Turkiye as a strategic adversary and interprets Turkiye’s capabilities as evidence of hostile intentions.
Al-Sharaa is seeking foreign policy support wherever he can find it, observes Scheller. “In recent months, Turkiye has increasingly become one of the countries from which Damascus expects concrete assistance.” This is not just a matter of security: Ankara wants to expand its regional influence and, at the same time, has an interest in maintaining stability along the shared border, she said.
Following the overthrow of Syria’s longtime ruler Bashar Assad in December 2024, Israel established a security zone north of the Golan Heights and has repeatedly attacked Syrian targets. According to an analysis by the Carnegie Foundation, the calls for such a buffer zone is deeply rooted in Israeli security thinking; less clear, however, is the intention — sometimes attributed to Israel by analysts — of permanently fragmenting Syria to keep it weak.
The US think tank FDD takes a different view, pointing to Israel’s skepticism toward the new Syrian military and Turkish support. However, Schneider notes that the new regime in Syria has extended a hand to Israel from the outset, despite its ideological origins. “Damascus does not want a war with Israel,” he said, adding that it wants to regain its national sovereignty. It is precisely this aspiration that clashes with Israel’s military presence and its red lines.
“Syria is caught between two militarily powerful neighbors that respect neither its sovereignty nor its territorial integrity,” said Scheller.
In her view, the outcome will now depend on al-Sharaa’s negotiating skills. “How can he defend Syrian sovereignty against these two neighbors and actually chart a distinct Syrian path?” However, Syria’s weakness does not lie solely in its military inferiority. The country must first develop a viable political order, she notes.
This is also the starting point for political scientist Haid Haid in an analysis for the British think tank Chatham House: “Syria’s foreign policy success has been significant, but it cannot, on its own, secure stability. In this sense, Syria’s greatest vulnerability lies not at its borders, but within.”

item.title: Death toll from Algeria wildfires rises to 12
item.description:
Forest fires killed 12 people and injured dozens in northeastern Algeria on Wednesday, the interior minister and civil protection authorities said.
The tolls rose from earlier local media reports of two deaths and an unspecified number of injuries in coastal Bejaia province, around 300 kilometers (190 miles) from the capital Algiers.
Five people were killed in Jijel province, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou province, Interior Minister Said Sayoud told national television.
A further 54 people were being treated for burns, including six serious cases, at a hospital in Bejaia, he said.
An eight-year-old boy and a 22-year-old woman were among those killed in Bejaia, a local radio station reported.
Sayoud and Health Minister Mohamed Seddik Ait Messaoudene had travelled to Bejaia to “assess the progress of firefighting operations on the ground... and the condition of the injured,” the official APS news agency reported.
Many residents in Bejaia and Jijel have been evacuated, according to the civil protection agency and local media.
As of 8pm (1900 GMT) on Wednesday, firefighters were battling 69 blazes, the civil protection agency said.
Images broadcast by local site Jijel News showed panicked residents taking refuge in a post office as thick clouds of smoke billowed around them.
Three major national highways connecting regions in the east of the country were closed due to forest fires near the cities of Bejaia, Jijel and Setif, the gendarmerie said.
The civil protection agency said it had deployed significant resources to combat the blazes, which are being fueled by strong winds.
Forest fires occur regularly in northern Algeria during the summer, but climate change is amplifying their impact by causing increasingly frequent droughts and intense heat.
More than 30 people were killed in July 2023 when fires tore through thousands of hectares of forests and farmland, as well as hundreds of homes, in the area around Bejaia.
Authorities recorded nearly 2,000 fires nationwide in July this year.
More than 100 people had to temporarily flee their homes in Annaba in late July as fires swept through the northeastern province, damaging nearly 150 homes.
Official investigations often end with arrests for suspected arson. Four people in Constantine province have been placed in pre-trial detention in connection with the July fires.

item.title: Germany reports record 15,800 heat-related deaths this summer
item.description:
Germany has registered a record 15,800 heat-related deaths this summer as Europe struggles through a series of punishing heatwaves, the national public health institute said Thursday.
The worst affected group were people over 75, and around 9,600 deaths were recorded in one week in late June when Germany baked in temperatures over 40°C, said the Robert Koch Institute (RKI).
Another 4,000 heat-related deaths were recorded between late July and mid-August, said the institute in its latest update.
Heat and drought have battered much of Europe this summer, fueling a spike in heat-related mortality, wildfires, devastating many crops and dropping water levels in major rivers. France, Britain and Spain have all reported thousands of excess summer deaths.
The institute said it has collected heat mortality data for the past decade and that the previous record was 8,900 deaths in 2018. A separate report by a medical publication had estimated 10,000 heat deaths in 1994.
Extreme heat can kill through heatstroke but mostly proves fatal when combined with existing conditions such as cardiovascular, lung or kidney diseases.
The RKI models heat-related mortality using statistical methods that compare deaths during summer weeks with and without heatwaves.
Climate change and heat adaptation were on the agenda of a two-day cabinet retreat this week led by conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz, but no new measures were announced.
Merz said Germany’s 16 states are primarily responsible for heat protection and are already set to receive 100 billion euros ($116 billion) over the next 12 years from a special infrastructure and climate protection fund.
“There is no shortage of programs or of funds,” Merz said Wednesday, adding that the government would examine potential aid for the agricultural and forestry sectors after drought and forest fires.
The parliamentary chief of Merz’s CDU party, Thorsten Frei, meanwhile rejected a proposal by center-left SPD ministers to anchor climate protection in the German constitution as a joint task of national, state and local governments.
This model would carry the risk “that one level of government points the finger at another, and ultimately little gets done,” he told Deutschlandfunk radio.
The group Environmental Action Germany charged the government was “irresponsible” because it had “failed to adopt a single effective measure for heat protection following an extreme summer that saw thousands of heat-related deaths.”
It urged legal changes and funding to help municipalities and cities unseal paved surfaces that store heat and to plant vastly more trees.
“Future summers will be even hotter,” said the group’s director Barbara Metz. “Yet instead of finally ensuring our cities remain livable and people stay healthy, the government is merely tinkering with the symptoms.”

item.title: Nazrul: Time needed to see election manifesto benefits
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Adviser and BNP Standing Committee member Nazrul Islam Khan has said people will have to wait some time to see the benefits of promises made in the election manifesto.
He made the remarks at a memorial meeting at the National Press Club on Thursday, marking the 11th death anniversary of former prime minister Kazi Zafar Ahmed.
“In the name of democracy, autocratic rule continued in the country for a long time. At present, the government has to shoulder the major responsibility of rebuilding the country and meeting people’s expectations,” Nazrul said.
He said the government wants to work with everyone to rebuild the country, adding that all political alliances and parties must exercise patience to make that possible.
“People have to be given some time to see the benefits of the promises made to them before the election,” he said.
“Given the current situation, there is no alternative to political parties working with mutual trust and patience,” Nazrul added.

item.title: Third session of 13th Parliament begins
item.description:
The third session of the 13th Parliament, formed through the February 12 election, began on Thursday afternoon after a 43-day recess.
The session began at 3pm with Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad in the chair.
Chief Whip Nurul Islam Moni on Wednesday said the formation of parliamentary standing committees and passage of key bills would receive top priority during the session.
The session may continue for five to 10 days, although its duration could be extended if necessary, he said.
The chief whip said around six important bills could be placed before the House during the session, including proposed laws concerning property transfers, enforced disappearances and human rights protection.
The President summoned the parliamentary session on August 11, exercising the powers vested in him under Article 72(1) of the Constitution.
Earlier, on July 15, the second, or budget, session of the current Parliament was prorogued after 27 working days.
During the session, Parliament passed a Tk 9,38,000 crore national budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year, the first budget under the current BNP government.
Parliament passed a total of 11 bills and formed 11 parliamentary committees during the session, including the Special Committee for Constitutional Amendment and nine parliamentary standing committees.
The first session of the 13th Parliament commenced on March 12, 2026.

item.title: Mirza Abbas acquitted in 15 corruption cases
item.description:
A Dhaka court has acquitted BNP Standing Committee member Mirza Abbas and 12 others in 15 cases involving alleged irregularities and corruption amounting to Tk127.64 crore in the allocation of 18 abandoned government houses.
Judge Muhammad Kamrul Hasan Khan of Dhaka Special Judge's Court-3 delivered the verdict on Thursday. Mirza Abbas's lawyer Md Shahinur Islam confirmed the matter.
According to court sources, the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) filed 15 separate cases against 21 people, including Mirza Abbas, over the alleged sale of 18 government houses without tenders.
Mirza Abbas and 11 others were accused in all 15 cases.
The ACC filed the cases on March 29, 2007. Following an investigation, charge sheets were submitted, and on September 25 of the same year, the then judge Shahed Nuruddin framed charges against the accused.
According to the charges, Rajuk had invited tenders for 18 abandoned government houses, but the process was allegedly manipulated to allocate the houses at unusually low prices, causing a government loss of Tk1,276,419,059.
The cases alleged that Mirza Abbas, then housing and public works minister, abused his power and exerted illegal influence to approve the sale of the houses through low-priced tenders arranged by Rajuk, despite higher valuations provided by Public Works Department executive engineers.
The accused were charged under Section 409 of the Penal Code, Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and Section 109 of the Penal Code.
According to case documents, the ACC filed the cases with Motijheel police station in March 2007, alleging that the 18 abandoned government houses in prime areas of the capital were sold at abnormally low prices through manipulated tenders during the BNP-Jamaat coalition government.
The charge sheets alleged that the accused benefited financially from the sales and that the government incurred a loss of Tk127.64 crore. The names of 14 additional accused were later included in the charge sheets for allegedly receiving benefits from the transactions.
The 15 cases relate to the allocation of the 18 houses. The ACC has filed seven appeals against High Court verdicts dismissing seven of the cases based on separate petitions by five individuals.
The five are Bashundhara Group Chairman Ahmed Akbar Sobhan, former Rajuk chief engineer Imdadul Islam, Ekom Engineering Company Ltd Managing Director Mehedi Hasan, Hasna Ahmed, wife of Chittagong Awami League leader Afsar Uddin Ahmed, and SM Anwar Hossain.
In addition, Bayrar Ali Haider Chowdhury filed a leave-to-appeal petition challenging the High Court's decision concerning the validity of the case. A hearing was held on the applications, while Ali Haider's leave-to-appeal petition was dismissed.
During the trial, the court recorded testimony from 23 of the 24 prosecution witnesses.
After a lengthy trial, the court acquitted all the accused of the charges on Thursday.

Have a small balcony? grow these seven useful herbs at home
item.description:
You do not need a large garden to grow fresh herbs at home. A few pots placed near a kitchen window, balcony, or another sunny spot can be enough to grow several useful varieties.
Besides adding flavor and aroma to food, many herbs contain antioxidants and other plant compounds that can contribute to a healthy diet. With regular care, you can simply pick fresh leaves whenever needed.
Rosemary is a fragrant herb widely used in cooking. It contains antioxidants such as rosmarinic acid, which may help protect cells from oxidative stress.
Rosemary does not like excessive water, so make sure the pot has proper drainage. It grows best with plenty of sunlight.
Fresh rosemary leaves can be used with meat, grilled or roasted vegetables, and baked dishes.
Basil is a popular herb that is relatively easy to grow at home. It contains antioxidant compounds such as eugenol, which may help protect the body from oxidative stress.
Basil can be grown from seeds or cuttings. It needs plenty of sunlight, while the soil should be watered when it begins to dry out.
Fresh basil can be added to salads, drinks, and various dishes. Keep in mind that different varieties of basil are not necessarily the same as the tulsi commonly grown in Bangladesh, so identify the variety before planting.
Thyme contains thymol and flavonoids, compounds known for their antioxidant properties. It is also commonly associated with supporting overall respiratory and immune health.
One advantage of thyme is that it requires relatively little care. It does not need frequent watering and can grow well in a pot with adequate sunlight.
Use fresh thyme in soups, stews, meat marinades, and other dishes.
Mint is one of the most familiar herbs in Bangladeshi kitchens. It contains menthol and other plant compounds and is commonly used to add a refreshing flavor to food and drinks.
Mint is relatively easy to grow and can thrive even in a small pot. However, it spreads quickly, so growing it in a separate container is a good idea.
Mint leaves can be used in tea, lemonade, salads, chutneys, fuchka sauces, and various dishes.
Oregano is particularly popular in pizza and pasta dishes. It contains antioxidant compounds such as carvacrol.
The herb generally grows well in sunny and relatively dry conditions. When growing oregano in a pot, place it somewhere that receives plenty of sunlight.
It can be used in pizza, pasta, pasta sauces, meat dishes, and other Italian or Mediterranean-style meals.
Parsley contains compounds such as apigenin and luteolin, as well as vitamin C. These nutrients and plant compounds have antioxidant properties and may contribute to overall health.
Unlike some other herbs, parsley can also be grown indoors if it receives moderate sunlight.
Fresh parsley can be added to soups, salads, and smoothies or used as a garnish for various dishes.
Sage contains polyphenols, which are known for their antioxidant properties. These compounds may help protect the body from oxidative stress.
Sage needs plenty of sunlight but does not require excessive watering. It can be grown in a pot on a balcony or beside a sunny window.
Its leaves have a distinctive earthy aroma and rich flavor and can be used in meat dishes, soups, and other savory foods.
Bangladesh's warm and humid climate means that not every herb will grow in exactly the same way. Before buying a plant, check its requirements for sunlight, watering, and soil.

Overall, these herbs can be a nutritious addition to a varied and balanced diet. However, no herb should be considered a substitute for medical treatment. Use them in moderation as part of a diverse diet rather than relying on them to prevent or treat disease.

item.title: Your hair is turning gray early, but why?
item.description:
Seeing gray or white strands before the age of 30 can be surprising, but premature graying is not always simply a result of getting older. Genetics, nutritional deficiencies, stress, smoking, and certain medical conditions can all contribute to hair losing its natural color.
Hair gets its color from a pigment called melanin, which is produced by specialized cells called melanocytes in the hair follicles. As these cells produce less melanin, new strands gradually appear gray or white.
If your parents or close family members started getting gray hair at a young age, you may be more likely to experience the same. The age at which graying begins and how quickly it progresses can vary considerably from person to person, and genetics plays an important role.
So, having gray hair at a young age does not automatically mean that something is wrong with your health.
Low levels of vitamin B12 have been associated with premature graying. Vitamin B12 is essential for several important processes in the body, and a deficiency can affect overall health as well as hair.
If you are experiencing premature graying along with other symptoms of nutritional deficiency, a healthcare professional may recommend appropriate blood tests.
Nutritional deficiencies may also contribute to premature graying. Research has linked low levels of nutrients such as iron and vitamin B12 with early loss of hair pigment. Some evidence also points to minerals such as copper and zinc, although the relationship is not as straightforward as genetics.
Copper, in particular, is involved in processes related to pigmentation, and copper deficiency can sometimes be associated with gray hair at a younger age.
Long-term or intense stress may also contribute to premature graying. Research suggests that the body's stress response can affect pigment-producing cells in hair follicles.
However, gray hair does not usually appear overnight because of a stressful event. The color of a strand is determined as it grows from the follicle, so the effects of stress may become noticeable later.
Premature graying can sometimes be associated with autoimmune conditions that affect pigment-producing cells, including vitiligo and alopecia areata. Certain genetic conditions and medications may also cause gray or white hair.
This does not mean that everyone with premature gray hair has an underlying illness. In many cases, genetics remains the primary explanation.
Once a hair follicle stops producing enough melanin, existing gray hair generally does not regain its original color naturally. However, if premature graying is related to a treatable nutritional deficiency or another underlying condition, addressing that problem may help slow further graying.
If you notice a sudden or unusually early increase in gray hair, avoid taking vitamin or mineral supplements without knowing whether you actually have a deficiency.
Instead, consult a doctor or dermatologist. Depending on your symptoms and medical history, they may recommend blood tests to check for nutritional deficiencies or other possible causes.
Bottom line: Premature gray hair is not necessarily a sign of poor health. Genetics is a major factor, while nutritional deficiencies, stress, smoking, and certain medical conditions may also contribute. Identifying the underlying cause is more useful than trying unproven remedies to restore hair color.
